newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish pound firms but still hostage to sterling.
newsitem.headline: Irish pound firms but still hostage to sterling.

text.p: The Irish pound clawed back some ground against sterling on Thursday, mainly due to early profit-taking in British currency, dealers said.
The Irish unit, which had dipped as low 0.8750 stg at one point on Wednesday, was trading at 0.8845 stg and 2.7046/86 marks by 1036 GMT on Thursday.
"The Irish pound is still very much a hostage to sterling," one currency dealer said. "Sterling has fallen from its highs of yesterday and has allowed the Irish to pick up a bit."
The dealer said the Irish pound's upward progress was hampered when sterling rebounded on UK trade statistics, which proved relatively insulated from the British currency's recent strength.
Britain's global trade deficit unexpectedly fell to 508 million stg in May from 989 million stg in April.
Against the mark, the dealer said he expected the Irish pound to run into good selling interest once it breached the key 2.7050 marks level.
"Generally there is good interest out there to sell the punt above 2.7050 marks," the dealer said. "This is a very tough resistence level to break."
"The punt has bounced today because sterling weakened on profit-taking," Riada economist Dan McLaughlin said. "I think the punt will stay around 88.50 stg today."

McLaughlin said while part of sterling's rise was due to cyclical moves, part of the reason for its strength was a more structural shift out of the mark because of EMU and the perception that the euro will be a weak currency.
"Although sterling could come back a bit if EMU stays on track, it is difficult to see sterling coming down in any dramatic way," McLaughlin said.
"So if sterling stays above 3.0 marks, which I suspect it will for quite a while, then the Irish will remain in this 88-89 pence stg range with a danger that we will slip below 88 pence again."
The domestic market shrugged off domestic official data which forecast Ireland's 1997 average inflation at two percent and GDP growth at 7.4 percent.
"Sterling is the key currency and that is what the market is focusing on."
